findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Maintained schools deficit balances increased to 24 schools (up from 21), with nursery sector crisis: 11 of 12 nursery schools in deficit totalling £5.5m.
findings.detail: The number of schools in cumulative deficit rose from 21 to 24 during 2025/26. Nursery schools are the critical issue: 11 of 12 maintained nursery schools are in deficit with a combined shortfall of £5.5m. The paper notes "some of these deficits represent a substantial proportion of their annual budgets". While the team reduced deficits by £0.9m during 2025/26, this was insufficient to prevent the position deteriorating.
findings.matters: Schools in deficit pose governance risk and may eventually require council bailout or closure. The concentration in nursery provision suggests either demographic pressure or unit cost issues. This is a leading indicator of broader DSG sustainability problems filtering down to maintained school sector.
findings.figures: 24 schools in deficit (up from 21), 11 of 12 nursery schools in deficit, £12.2m cumulative school deficits, £5.5m nursery deficit
findings.quote: Out of 24 schools sharing the end of year cumulative deficit position of £12.2 million, the nursery sector continues to be a concern, with 11 out of 12 maintained nursery schools in a deficit position which totals £5.5 million. findings.matters: Commercial property income is volatile and the council is over-reliant on it. findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: HRA housing arrears rose significantly, with 77% of the increase since NEC system implementation in October 2025.
findings.detail: HRA housing debt increased by £0.526m across the year, driven by rising arrears in current rent and former tenant arrears. However, 77% of this increase (approximately £0.405m) accrued in just 5 months following the NEC system implementation from 21 October 2025 onwards. Emergency accommodation and temporary accommodation properties contributed significantly to the rise. The council is procuring new caseload management software to address this.
findings.matters: System implementation failures are causing deterioration in rent collection and arrears management, directly impacting HRA cash flow. The acceleration of arrears post-implementation suggests the issue is system-driven rather than demand-driven, but indicates operational control issues during the transition. Future collection performance and HRA income depends on new software working.
findings.figures: Total HRA debt rise £0.526m, 77% (£0.405m) since October 2025 NEC implementation
findings.quote: The total HRA debt has risen in 2025/26 led by an increase in arrears for current rent and former arrears. This reflects challenges experienced due to the implementation of NEC housing management system, UC migration and changes to our ability to manage possession cases since October. Of the total increase, 77% has accrued since the implementation of NEC.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Council tax collection declined to 93.5% from 94%, with pressures from discounts, exemptions and cost-of-living impacts.
findings.detail: Collection rate fell by 0.5 percentage points despite an in-year surplus of £3.9m (from changes in CTR and some improved arrears recovery). However, the Council explicitly flags "adverse pressures from discounts and exemptions, including single person discounts and non‑student related exemptions". This suggests structural pressures from eligibility/vulnerability rather than temporary collection issues.
findings.matters: Declining council tax collection rates, combined with rising exemptions, indicate household financial stress and may signal deteriorating collection sustainability. This feeds directly into General Fund cash and 2026/27 budget planning.
findings.figures: 93.5% collection (2025/26) vs 94% (2024/25), £3.9m in-year surplus
findings.quote: During the year, the estimate of council tax income was revised to reflect a range of in‑year movements within the Collection Fund. This included changes in the Council Tax Reduction Scheme caseload, movements in discounts and exemptions, and the impact of premiums. While there were favourable movements arising from reductions in Council Tax Reduction Scheme claims and improved arrears recovery, these were offset by adverse pressures from discounts and exemptions, including single person discounts and non‑student related exemptions.

The council notes this "will impact the 2026/27 financial year through the Collection Fund". This is separate from council tax collection, which also deteriorated.
findings.matters: Business rates deficits create in-year cash pressures and reduce core funding available in the following year. A £10.7m impact to 2026/27 comes precisely when the council is facing structural pressures in children's and adult services and ambitious savings targets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £3.8m in a £207m budget, with ongoing pressures from demand, complexity and inflation in provider fees.
findings.detail: Despite a £14.5m savings programme, ASC spent £3.8m more than its revised budget (2%). The paper notes "sustained demand and increasing complexity among those drawing on care and support". Specific pressures come from residential care (£4.9m overspend), nursing care (£4.3m), and supported accommodation (£6m), only partially offset by underspends in non-residential services. The council explicitly warns that future years require "savings of circa £8 million to support ongoing financial sustainability" against "continued inflationary pressures on provider fees and pay".
findings.matters: Adult social care is both a growth cost (demographic and demand-driven) and inflation-sensitive (provider-fee dependent). Overspend despite ambitious transformation indicates the council cannot keep pace with cost drivers, and 2026/27 target of £8m additional savings may not be achievable if provider fees and demand continue to rise.
findings.figures: £3.8m overspend on £207.4m revised budget, £14.5m savings programme, £8m target for 2026/27
findings.quote: Adult Social Care (ASC) reported an overall overspend of £3.8 million against their revised net budget of £207.4 million. During 2025/36, Adult Social Care (ASC) took a range of proactive steps to help mitigate rising cost pressures and reduce budgetary overspends. Despite these actions, the final outturn was an overspend of £3.8 million against a revised net budget of £207.4 million, underlining the need for work to achieve a financially sustainable position to continue at pace.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Savings delivery only 93% achieved: £4.3m shortfall in 2025/26 with £6.9m carrying forward at risk into 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council delivered £55m of its £59.3m savings target (93%). The £4.3m shortfall was covered by contingency. However, £6.9m of under-delivered or over-delivered savings will carry forward into 2026/27 (£5.9m General Fund, £1m HRA), which the council states "will carry forward into 2026/27 and either be managed through the budget set for 2026/27 or will continue to be required to support delivery of the balanced budget". This suggests the council is already tight on 2026/27 delivery.
findings.matters: A 7% saving-delivery gap reveals execution risk on future year budgets. The language around carry-forwards being "required to support delivery of the balanced budget" indicates these are not optional savings but essential to balance. Combined with new growth in demand-led costs, this creates sustainability risk.
findings.figures: £59.3m total target, £55m delivered (93%), £4.3m shortfall, £6.9m carrying forward
findings.quote: Against this target, £55 million (93%) are reported as delivered with £4.3 million (7%) not being achieved in year. The impact of this has been mitigated during the year through application of £4.3 million of budget delivery contingency.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A1a - BCC 2025-26 Provisional Outturn - Revenue
findings.headline: Children and Families General Fund overspend of £14.5m driven by rising placement numbers and external provider costs.
findings.detail: Children's services overspent by £14.5m (10% of revised budget) with the largest pressure in Strategic Improvement and Collaboration (£9.6m overspend). The paper explicitly states this is "largely due to increasing numbers of children entering care and increases in costs of placements, particularly for those children placed with external providers". An additional £16m in savings is planned for 2026/27 through the Stable Homes programme, but the council notes "the directorate is carrying additional pressures relating to an increase in care starts at the end of 2025/26", flagging risk to delivery.
findings.matters: This is a growing structural cost pressure driven by demand (increasing care starts) and market inflation (provider costs). It demonstrates the council cannot currently contain these costs within existing budgets, and future year savings targets depend on a transformation programme that is already at risk from continued placement growth.
findings.figures: £14.5m overspend (10% of £148.7m revised budget), £16m savings target for 2026/27
findings.quote: The full year overspend includes £9.6 million overspend in Strategic Improvement and Collaboration, £4.8 million in Children and Families and £0.1 million in Education, Inclusion and Skills. This position does not include the Dedicated Schools Grant (set out at section 4) which is currently showing a £44.7 million deficit.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £44.7m and cumulative DSG crisis of £138m, driven by High Needs placement costs exceeding funding.

findings.paper_title: 17 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025_26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit partially addressed by proposed £100m SEND reform funding, but timing uncertain

A £53.7m capital programme to create 392 new SEN places by 2030 is underway, but only 84 places (22%) have been delivered so far.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a known systemic issue across local government (Office of Budgetary Responsibility estimates £14bn total UK deficit by March 2028). The capital programme's slow delivery rate (22% complete) suggests execution risk in the solution.
findings.figures: Proposed £100m additional funding; would reduce deficit by 90%; £53.7m capital programme 2024–2030; 84 of 392 places delivered (22%); OBR estimates £14bn total UK deficit by March 2028
findings.quote: This is principally a finance issue with central government supplying insufficient funding, through the High Needs Block of the DSG, to fund the council's statutory responsibilities. The issue is not Bristol specific with numerous local authorities also seeing high deficits. The Office of Budgetary Responsibility estimates the total High Needs deficit across the UK will be £14 billion by 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: 17 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025_26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: Outstanding debt held at over £200m throughout 2025/26
findings.detail: The council's outstanding debt levels remained above £200m during 2025/26. While the Managing Our Debt programme has made improvements in accounts receivable (30% reduction, 67% reduction in older debts, in-year collection rate up to 85.6%), the council describes collection levels as now a critical success measure for overall financial health.
findings.matters: Debt at this scale affects cash flow and working capital management. The emphasis on collection as critical to financial health suggests the council depends on revenue recovery to balance its budget.
findings.figures: £200m+ outstanding; AR indebtedness down 30%; debts before 1/4/25 down 67%; in-year collection rate 85.6% (up from 74.2%); average debtor days 55 (was 77)
findings.quote: The council's outstanding debt levels has held at over £200m over 2025/26. Through the managing our debt programme there has been significant improvement in accounts receivable debt. As our tax base has grown the level of arrears for council Tax and business rates has increased, through the fairer funding review and local government settlement we are now more reliant on the collection of local tax making collection levels a critical success measure for the financial health of the council.

findings.paper_title: 17 - Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025_26 - Appendix A
findings.headline: 2026/27 requires £41m of savings, with another £29m needed from 2027/28 to 2030/31
findings.detail: The council's spending exceeds available funding. The approved 2026/27 budget requires £41m of savings, and the five-year plan identifies an additional £29m of savings needed from 2027/28 to 2030/31. The paper identifies this as a significant issue and notes the council is improving budget monitoring processes to ensure consistent tracking of savings delivery against wider budget management.
findings.matters: A £70m+ savings requirement across the MTFP period indicates acute financial pressure. The fact that the council is upgrading monitoring processes suggests prior concern about savings slippage.
findings.quote: With the cost of operating the council exceeding available funding, the delivery of savings and income generation plans remain as a significant issue. The 2026/27 budget approved in February 2026 requires £41m of savings to be delivered. The future years financial plan from 2027/28 to 2030/31 has identified a savings requirement of £29m in addition to the £41m.

findings.paper_title: Final Audit Committee Risk Management Report Q4 25_26
findings.headline: Construction safety management risk deteriorating following multiple contractor near-miss incidents.
findings.detail: The Construction Design Management framework risk has escalated from a score of 10 to 15 (likelihood increasing from Unlikely to Likely) due to three contractor incidents in recent months. The report notes these incidents 'could have resulted in serious or fatal outcomes,' indicating actual failures in the council's contractor oversight mechanisms.
findings.matters: Repeat near-miss incidents (three in recent months) demonstrate that risk controls are not preventing failures. This represents potential legal liability and signals governance weaknesses in operational risk management that extend beyond this single category.
findings.figures: CRR61 score increased from 2 × 5 = 10 to 3 × 5 = 15; three contractor incidents in recent months with potential serious or fatal consequences
findings.quote: There have been 3 poor contractor incidents across the Council in the last few months where the outcomes could have resulted in serious or fatal outcomes.

findings.paper_title: Final Audit Committee Risk Management Report Q4 25_26
findings.headline: Two Critical-level risks threaten housing standards compliance and infrastructure asset maintenance.
findings.detail: Bristol identifies two Critical-rated threats (the highest severity level, each scoring 7 × 4 = 28): HRA stock failing to meet landlord statutory obligations and decent homes standards, which could trigger regulatory enforcement action; and inability to adequately maintain and replace highway, traffic, parking and docks infrastructure assets. Both are assessed as Almost Certain in likelihood.
findings.matters: Regulatory enforcement on housing standards and infrastructure maintenance failures directly threaten service delivery capacity and create contingent liabilities. Lenders need assurance that councils can sustain core asset management and meet statutory obligations.
findings.figures: 2 Critical Threat risks at 7 × 4 = 28 severity; 5 High risks; 7 Medium risks
findings.quote: There are two Critical Threat risks scoring Critical 7 x Almost Certain 4 = 28. CRR60 – Failure of HRA stock to meet landlord statutory obligations, the decent homes standard and consumer standards may lead to regulatory enforcement action. CRR58 Unable to adequately maintain and replace the Highway, Traffic, Parking and Docks infrastructure assets

findings.headline: £44.7 million in-year DSG deficit with £138 million cumulative carry-forward
findings.detail: Bristol has a £44.7 million deficit in the current year (ending March 2026). Added to the £88.7 million brought forward from the previous year, this creates a £138 million cumulative deficit. Although the DfE Safety Valve agreement provides £26.130 million safety valve funding and a separate £21.9 million reserve, the revised deficit still stands at £85.4 million after these mitigations. The General Fund Reserve contributed £15.175 million in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A large and growing DSG deficit, only partially mitigated by extraordinary DfE safety valve support, indicates structural underfunding and reliance on external support to manage education budgets
findings.figures: In-year deficit: £44.7 million; cumulative carry-forward: £138.0 million; after Safety Valve mitigation: £85.4 million; Safety Valve funding: £26.130m; General Fund reserve: £21.9 million
findings.quote: The in-year deficit on the DSG at Period 12 is £44.7 million. However, as part of the DfE Safety Valve agreement, the General Fund also holds a separate reserve which stands at £21.9 million at 31 March.

findings.headline: Number of schools in cumulative deficit increased from 21 to 24 in one year
findings.detail: The proportion of maintained schools in deficit worsened year-on-year, increasing from 21 schools at the start of 2025/26 to 24 by year end. The cumulative deficit across these 24 schools stands at £12.2 million. The overall maintained schools position deteriorated from a net deficit of £5.9 million at year start to £6.6 million at year end.
findings.matters: A worsening trend in the number and extent of school deficits suggests increasing financial stress across the school system and potential growing need for council support
findings.figures: Schools in cumulative deficit: 21 in 2024/25 to 24 in 2025/26 (increase of 3); cumulative deficit across 24 schools: £12.2 million; overall maintained schools position: £5.9m deficit to £6.6m deficit
findings.quote: By the end of the year, 24 schools, an increase of 3 from 21 in 2024/25, shared a cumulative deficit position of £12.2 million

findings.headline: Nursery schools: 11 of 12 in cumulative deficit with £5.5 million total deficit
findings.detail: The nursery sector is flagged as 'a concern' with 11 out of 12 maintained nursery schools in deficit totaling £5.548m. The paper states 'some of these deficits represent a substantial proportion of their annual budgets.' Although the council reduced accumulated deficits by £0.9 million in 2025/26, 11 schools remain in deficit and work will continue to reduce deficits further.
findings.matters: Persistent deficits in 92% of a school sector, with significant budget shortfalls, suggests either unaffordable service delivery or sustained need for council subsidy
findings.figures: Nursery deficit: £5.548 million (closing balance); 11 of 12 schools in deficit; £0.9 million reduction in accumulated deficits achieved in 2025/26
findings.quote: 11 out of 12 maintained nursery schools in a deficit position which totals £5.5 million. Some of these deficits represent a substantial proportion of their annual budgets.

findings.headline: High Needs Block cost exceeding funding is the largest DSG pressure
findings.detail: The paper identifies the High Needs Block as 'the largest pressure' in the DSG, with the cost of placing children with high needs continuing to exceed available funding. The council is dependent on DfE approval of its Local SEND Reform Plan to access additional High Needs Stability Grant funding. This is an ongoing structural mismatch, not a one-off issue.
findings.matters: A structural deficit in a major cost area (£96.091m allocation), dependent on external approval for funding solutions, indicates unresolved financial pressure affecting the council's overall position
findings.figures: High Needs Block allocation: £96.091 million out of total DSG £546.784 million
findings.quote: The largest pressure continues to be within the High Needs Block as a result of the cost of placing children with high needs exceeding the available funding.

findings.headline: General Fund financing cost ratio rising to 8.3% in 2026/27, driven by capital investment and Invest to Save schemes
findings.detail: The General Fund financing cost ratio is rising from 7.2% (24/25) to 8.3% (26/27), then falling gradually to 7.1% by 30/31 due to forecast increases in revenue support grants. The document cites both core capital programmes and 'Invest to Save Projects' as drivers. Invest to Save schemes typically rely on income streams (e.g. from property, commercial activity, or energy savings) to service debt; if those income streams fail to materialize or fall short, the council will face a revenue shortfall.
findings.matters: An s151 officer needs to verify that each Invest to Save project has a credible, audited income projection and contingency plan. A lender will want to see that the underlying assets are sound and the income is not dependent on speculative assumptions (e.g., property values, occupancy rates). The fact that these are mentioned only in passing, without itemization, is a flag.
findings.figures: General Fund financing cost: 7.2% (24/25), 8.1% (25/26), 8.3% (26/27); thereafter declining
findings.quote: The above ratio's are increasing for both the General Fund and HRA to reflect the additional borrowing being undertaken to support the delivery of the capital programme, including the new Invest to Save Projects and Housing new build programme.

findings.headline: Interest rates forecast to remain elevated longer than previously expected, increasing refinancing risk
findings.detail: The council explicitly states that 'Interest rate forecasts are forecast to remain higher and for longer than previously reported due to concerns around inflation and annual wage growth'. While the strategy assumes rates will fall (Bank Rate from 3.75% to 3.25%), the document flags 'significant risks' including wage growth, domestic economic performance, and geopolitical factors. This uncertainty led the council to extend short-term borrowing maturity limits from 40% to 60% for 12–24 month tenors to avoid locking into longer-dated debt.
findings.matters: The council is betting on interest rate falls; if inflation persists or rates remain sticky, the cost of the planned £536m borrowing will be substantially higher than forecast. With an uncertain economic backdrop (US tariff policies, geopolitical events), this is a material refinancing risk. The shift to shorter maturities also means more frequent refinancing — another source of uncertainty for lenders.
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast: 3.75% (Mar 2026) to 3.25% (Mar 2028); PWLB 5-year rates forecast to fall from 4.60% to 4.10%; short-term borrowing limits increased from 40% to 60% for 12–24 month maturities
findings.quote: Interest rate forecasts are forecast to remain higher and for longer than previously reported due to concerns around inflation and annual wage growth... There are risks to these forecasts as set out in Annex 2: Economic Forecast and Interest Rate Forecast.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs more than doubling over the MTFS to 11.4% of revenue by 2030/31
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account financing cost ratio is forecast to rise from 5.7% in 2024/25 to 11.4% by 2030/31. This reflects the council's decision to fund a substantial housing new build programme through borrowing, with external HRA debt growing from £301m to £621m. The council explicitly notes this rising burden is driven by 'additional borrowing being undertaken to support the delivery of the capital programme, including the new Invest to Save Projects and Housing new build programme'.
findings.matters: A lender would flag this trajectory as unsustainable: by 2030/31, more than 1 in 10 HRA revenue will be consumed by financing costs before any housing management activity. This reduces flexibility to manage service pressures or maintain investment standards without raising rents or cutting services. For an s151 officer, this is a binding constraint on future HRA discretion.
findings.figures: 5.7% (24/25 actual) rising to 11.4% (30/31 estimate); HRA CFR growing from £252m to £621m over the same period
findings.quote: The above ratio's are increasing for both the General Fund and HRA to reflect the additional borrowing being undertaken to support the delivery of the capital programme, including the new Invest to Save Projects and Housing new build programme.

findings.headline: Schools funding deficit carries over under temporary statutory override until March 2028
findings.detail: The council has entered a Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education to address a deficit in Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) spending. This deficit is currently held in a separate reserve under a statutory override that expires on 31 March 2028. After that date, the council must ensure it has adequate usable reserves to cover any remaining DSG deficit and must have a clear plan for sustainability.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that Bristol has a known structural overspend in schools funding that is currently accommodated by government but will become the council's own reserve liability in 2028. This directly affects reserve adequacy planning and the council's medium-term financial resilience.
findings.figures: DSG deficit override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The SI has since been extended but remains time-limited now running until 31 March 2028 and the council therefore would have to ensure there are adequate usable reserves to cover any DSG deficit and a clear plan for sustainability when preparing the council's accounts beyond 2028. The council has entered into a Safety Valve agreement with the Department for Education and is actively working to address the medium term financial strategy deficit in the DSG.

findings.headline: Void losses (empty properties) forecast at £1.7m for 2025/26; planned reduction will not be met
findings.detail: Bad debt and void losses continue to be a material drain. Void loss forecast £1.7m for 2025/26, with void turnaround at ~82 days. The plan targets 65 days by 2026/27 then 5-day annual reductions thereafter. The document notes 'the planned reduction against void losses for 2025/26 will not be met', showing a structural issue in getting properties ready to let.
findings.matters: Voids represent lost rental income and opportunity cost. Persistent failure to meet targets suggests operational or market constraints that could worsen if demand softens.
findings.figures: Void loss 2025/26: £1.7m forecast; void turnaround 82 days actual vs 65-day target for 2026/27. Bad debt £2.0m (1.37% of dwelling rent).
findings.quote: Void Losses are currently forecast at circa £1.7 million for 2025/26. The planned reduction against void losses for 2025/26 will not be met, however the position has improved over previous years, with void turnaround at circa 82 days.

findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio in year 1 is 1.36, only 0.11 above minimum covenant, with significant year-on-year exposure to interest rate shocks
findings.detail: The HRA's Interest Cover Ratio (minimum 1.25) is 1.36 in 2026/27 (0.11 above minimum). The council proposes adding a 'comfort' requirement of £5m headroom from years 1–4 to protect against 'unknown shocks'. However, stress testing shows that if interest rates rise 1% across all new borrowing, the ICR would breach the 1.25 minimum. The plan shows 'comfort against ICR' only from year 2 onwards.
findings.matters: ICR covenant breach would trigger default on the HRA's borrowing terms and force immediate corrective action (savings or capital cuts). The narrow headroom leaves no tolerance for rate rises or income shortfalls.
findings.figures: ICR 2026/27: 1.36 (minimum 1.25); proposed comfort margin £5m; interest headroom year 1 £0.93m. Sensitivity: 1% rate rise in years 1–3 causes breach of covenant.
findings.quote: In order to combat this, it is proposed to introduce a minimum 'comfort' requirement against the ICR of up to £5 million from year 1 to year 4 (2029/30), at which point there is sufficient excess coverage to enable this to happen and still provide further capacity to invest.

findings.headline: High-rise block investment is deferred; four buildings (Dove Street, St Judes, Vincent Close, Ropewalk) have constrained funding
findings.detail: The risk register identifies four high-rise blocks with 'financial & deliverability constraints preventing investment'. The council plans asset and fire surveys to 'establish Asset Strategies for the high-rise blocks, starting with Barton House, St Judes, Vincent Close & Dove Street' to develop 'short and long-term investment plans'. This signals known but uncosted liabilities in the stock.
findings.matters: Building safety and fire safety requirements are regulatory. Deferring investment in known problem buildings increases risk of emergency costs (as shown by Barton House history).
findings.figures: Four named high-rise blocks with constrained funding. Previous Barton House emergency: £53m in-year pressure. Asset surveys being scheduled to quantify investment need.
findings.quote: The probability of this type of event occurring is increased with the financial & deliverability constraints preventing investment in Dove Street, St Judes, Vincent Close and Ropewalk.

findings.headline: Budget contains £4.6m savings target with no established programme, and minimal financial resilience
findings.detail: Achieving a balanced budget required including £4.6m of unidentified 'revenue efficiency and savings programme' in 2026/27. The document notes 'failure to deliver the programme will lead to safety-driven investment being reduced due to lack of financial resilience'. The HRA operating reserve of £44.3m (minimum £27.9m) leaves only £16.4m headroom, insufficient to absorb emergencies like the Barton House evacuation (which created £53m in-year pressure in 2024/25).
findings.matters: A £4.6m unplanned savings shortfall would force immediate capital cuts. The council's recent experience (£53m emergency in 2024/25) shows that unforeseen costs are material and likely.
findings.figures: Required savings £4.6m; operating reserve £44.3m with minimum £27.9m (headroom £16.4m); previous year emergency pressure £53m. Stress testing shows low financial resilience is a 'significant risk'.
findings.quote: Failure to deliver savings: the required £4.6m revenue savings will be challenging to deliver due to there being no previous programme established. Failure to deliver the programme will lead to safety driven (eg must do) investment being reduced due to the lack of financial resilience.

findings.headline: New borrowing requirement increased 81% in one year: £374.7m (up from £207.0m), with interest rates assumed at 4.5% but market rates already 4.6–6.2%
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumes £374.7m new borrowing over the plan period, up sharply from £207m in the previous year's plan. Interest is assumed at 4.5% throughout. However, PWLB maturity rates currently range 4.57–6.19%, and the council notes this 4.5% rate 'may be optimistic if longer-term loans are intended'. Total debt projected to rise from £245m to £619.3m. A 1% rise in rates would trigger breach of Interest Cover Ratio covenants.
findings.matters: Interest rate risk is material. Actual borrowing costs could be significantly higher than assumed, which would constrain the ability to fund capital work or maintain minimum reserves.
findings.figures: New borrowing £374.7m; total projected debt £619.3m (vs current £245m). Assumed rate 4.5%; market PWLB rates 4.57–6.19%. Sensitivity: each 1% rate rise reduces ICR below minimum (1.25) covenant by year 3. Interest headroom year 1: £0.93m.
findings.quote: At the time of writing, PWLB maturity loan rates vary from 4.57% to 6.19% depending upon the term of the loan, and annuity rates range from 4.60% to 6.19%. The current reduced HRA rate at 60 basis points below the standard PWLB lending rates is applicable until at least March 2026, with announcements about any further extension now anticipated in January 2026... may be optimistic if longer-term loans are intended.

findings.headline: Housing stock condition remains unmeasured; budget is interim and capital investment needs unknown
findings.detail: The council describes this budget as 'interim' pending completion of a full stock condition survey scheduled for 2027/28. Until then, the investment plan is constrained and 'it would be unwise to commit to investment spend that may become undeliverable and/or unviable'. This creates planning risk: once condition data arrives in 2027/28, the capital programme may need material revision. Current benchmarks suggest investment of £69,000–£75,900 per property; the interim plan is below this.
findings.matters: A major stock condition survey in 2027/28 could reveal liabilities that force borrowing up or capital plans to be rescaled. The council is deferring investment decisions that could affect long-term financial viability.
findings.figures: Benchmark investment £69,000–£75,900 per property; interim plan below this level. Stock condition survey completion expected 2027/28. New build programme: 1,109 homes over MTFP (described as 'significant reduction against previous Business Plans').
findings.quote: Once this intelligence is received and understood, the appropriate plans will be drawn up for future investment in existing stock and new delivery. Until such time, it would be unwise to commit to investment spend that may become undeliverable and/or unviable during the intervening period.

findings.headline: Supervision & Management costs surge £5.2m, driven by insurance premiums rising £1.6m
findings.detail: The largest budget pressure is a £5.2m increase in Supervision & Management (16% rise). Of this, £1.6m is insurance premium increases 'as previously reported throughout 2025/26', plus £0.9m for a new lone working system and £1.4m inflation. This appears to reflect realized costs that were forecast but are now built into baseline.
findings.matters: Insurance costs are a structural liability that constrains the HRA's ability to invest. If premiums continue rising, further savings would be forced.
findings.figures: Insurance premium increase £1.6m; new lone working system £0.9m; total Supervision & Management increase £5.2m (from £46.4m to £50.4m).
findings.quote: Supervision & Management - £5.2 million increase. This relates to a significant increase in insurance premiums (£1.6m) as previously reported throughout 2025/26, as well as additional costs relating to transforming services, a new lone working system (£0.9m) and inflationary increases of £1.4 million

findings.headline: Financial stabilization reversed: budget now depends entirely on government rent convergence policy not yet announced
findings.detail: The HRA improved dramatically from £12.5m overspend in 2024/25 to £0.5m in 2025/26. However, the 2026/27 budget excludes rent convergence income (worth £1.4–£2.8m annually depending on policy), deferring this to 2027/28 onwards. The government announcement, originally expected November 2025, is now delayed to January 2026 and 'still to be made'. Without convergence, the budget assumes baseline CPI+1%, but sensitivity analysis shows no convergence would be 'significantly negative' for the plan.
findings.matters: A policy change from government could force immediate budget revision and deferred capital spending. The council is projecting surpluses beyond 2027/28 only if convergence proceeds.
findings.figures: Budget includes no convergence income in 2026/27; £1.4m (at £1/week) or £2.8m (at £2/week) would be available from 2027/28 if policy proceeds. Stress test shows convergence removal causes 'significantly negative impact on business plan with reduction in revenue resources and increased borrowing need'.
findings.quote: An announcement was expected on rent convergence as part of the Autumn Statement in November 2025, however this has been delayed until January 2026, and at the time of writing, any announcement is still to be made.

findings.headline: Total identified risk exposure of £150.83m, with £28m drawn from unallocated reserves
findings.detail: The council has identified total financial risks of £150.83m across the estate. Of this, £28m is to be covered from unallocated general fund reserves (UR), while £108.83m sits as mitigating actions and £9m as corporate contingency. The reliance on unallocated reserves to cover identified risks reduces financial headroom.
findings.matters: Heavy reliance on unallocated reserves to cover known risks leaves the council with reduced flexibility for unforeseen events and signals tight budget planning.
findings.figures: £150.83m total risk impact; £28.00m from unallocated reserves; £108.83m from mitigating actions; £9.00m from corporate contingency; £5.00m from earmarked reserves
findings.quote: Mitigating Action – Strategic Directors / Directors to identify alternative measures to manage risks / opportunities within available resources and growth allocated as per budget report

findings.headline: Highway and infrastructure maintenance backlog rated as highest-probability risk (4x7=28)
findings.detail: Bristol is unable to adequately maintain and replace highway, traffic, parking and docks infrastructure assets, rated as the highest-probability/consequence risk on the register (28/35). The council has set aside £9m in corporate contingency for this.
findings.matters: Deferred infrastructure maintenance increases long-term capital costs, creates service quality/safety issues, and signals operational control problems to lenders.
findings.figures: £9.00m corporate contingency allocation; risk rating 4x7=28
findings.quote: Unable to adequately maintain and replace the Highway, Traffic, Parking and Docks infrastructure assets

findings.headline: Insurance cover gap exposes council to £30m potential uninsured loss liability
findings.detail: The register identifies a £30m risk that the council may not have appropriate insurance cover, leaving it exposed to self-funding losses from uninsured events or incidents. This is the second-largest single financial exposure on the register.
findings.matters: Uninsured losses create sudden budget shocks outside normal service delivery; a major incident could force large unplanned reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £30.00m financial impact
findings.quote: Possible failure to have appropriate insurance cover which may lead to budget shocks from Council self funding losses

findings.headline: Council has identified £8.25m risk of in-year financial deficit
findings.detail: The financial risks register explicitly names 'Possible In-Year Financial Deficit' as a risk with £8.25m exposure, indicating budget pressures exist in the current financial year that could require in-year action or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: In-year deficits force reactive spending cuts or reserve use, reducing financial flexibility and signalling budget control issues to lenders.
findings.figures: £8.25m mitigation cost set aside
findings.quote: Possible In-Year Financial Deficit

findings.headline: Adult Social Care faces £15m sustainability risk from national and local pressures
findings.detail: ASC is flagged as potentially financially unsustainable (risk rating 21/35), with a £15m financial impact. The risk stems from both national pressures on social care and local demand. This threatens the council's ability to deliver statutory duties in this area.
findings.matters: ASC is a statutory service. Financial unsustainability could force service reductions, provider collapse, or unplanned budget overruns that destabilise the council.
findings.figures: £15.00m financial impact; risk rating 3x7=21
findings.quote: ASC may be financially unsustainable due to national and local pressures, leading to a failure to deliver statutory duties

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit could revert to general fund from April 2026 if ringfence not extended
findings.detail: The council faces a £46.5m financial exposure if the statutory instrument ringfencing DSG deficits is not extended beyond March 2026. This is Bristol's single largest identified risk, as the deficit would then reverse into the general fund account and impact core budget. The risk is currently unmitigated (marked UR = unallocated reserve).
findings.matters: A £46.5m general fund charge would be a severe shock to Bristol's budget flexibility and borrowing capacity. This is a legislative cliff edge outside the council's control.
findings.figures: £46.50m financial impact; risk rating 3x7=21
findings.quote: Risk that the Statutory Instrument (2020/1212 and 2022/1328) related to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), which ringfences the deficit to the DSG is not extended beyond March 2026 and therefore reverts to the General Fund account.

findings.headline: Multiple savings reverse or disappear in later years, indicating one-off solutions not structural reform
findings.detail: Several proposals show negative figures in later years: transport (£1,163k reversal in 28/29), Clean Air Zone charge (£400k reversal in 29/30), homes and housing (£1,027k reversal in 29/30), strategy and resources (£1,000k reversal in 27/28). These reversals suggest the council is using short-term fixes to balance the current year, not delivering lasting savings.
findings.matters: A budget plan that requires reversals in year 3 or 4 suggests the council knows it cannot sustain these savings. The real budget problem is deferred, not solved.
findings.figures: £1,163k (transport), £1,027k (housing), £1,000k (strategy/resources), £400k (CAZ charge) reversals in future years
findings.quote: Alternative investment in sustainable transport — In 2026 to 2027, the council could use more funds left over from Clean Air Zone charges... [reverses to (£1,000k) in 27/28]

findings.headline: Significant budget savings depend on income that could fall in economic downturn
findings.detail: The council is counting on: planning application income exceeding targets (£200k), Clean Air Zone revenue (£200k), dividend income rising (£500k), and business rates pool funds being released (£1,077k). These income-dependent savings total at least £2,000k but have no cushion if the economy weakens.
findings.matters: Lenders care whether savings plans stay intact if the economy slows; these savings would be the first to disappear.
findings.figures: £200k planning; £200k CAZ; £500k dividend; £1,077k business rates pool; total £1,977k
findings.quote: Income from planning applications has exceeded income targets and is expected to continue to do so.

findings.headline: Large employer pension contribution saving depends on investment performance, not operational change
findings.detail: The council is proposing to save £7,200k in 2026/27 (and only 2026/27) by reducing employer pension contributions. The reason: the 2025 pension valuation showed positive investment performance, expected to lower the contribution rate. This is a one-off, purely financial gain, not a structural saving.
findings.matters: If investment returns reverse, this £7,200k saving disappears instantly, creating a sudden budget gap. It's not a resilient savings plan.
findings.quote: This is due to positive investment performance, which is expected to lead to a reduction in the employer contribution rate and remove the need for deficit contributions

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation driving repeated expensive solutions, signalling unresolved budget pressure
findings.detail: The council is pursuing multiple simultaneous approaches to temporary accommodation: a 40-year finance lease for 250 homes (£2,671k), purchase of 75 properties (£1,059k), long-term leasing of properties (£300k), partnership housing delivery (£436k). The cheaper option (direct lets with private landlords worth £2,430k) has been removed. This pattern across five years suggests the council is unable to sustainably solve temporary accommodation costs and is instead cycling through increasingly complex financing structures.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a growing budget pressure in many councils; Bristol's commitment to multiple long-term finance arrangements (including a 40-year lease) locks in spending. In a downturn, these become fixed costs.
findings.figures: £2,671k (finance lease); £1,059k (property purchase); £300k (leasing); £436k (partnership housing); £2,430k removed (direct lets option)
findings.quote: The council is looking at entering into a 40-year finance deal (with options to leave every 10 years) to secure 250 homes for temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: Multiple significant savings proposals have been removed or adjusted through separate budget appendix
findings.detail: At least seven major savings proposals are marked as "Saving removed though Appendix 10 budget adjustment": St Nicholas Market fees (£150k), non-recyclable waste collections (£1,000k), Cultural Investment Programme (£635k), child's homes operating model (£400k), temporary accommodation with private sector landlords (£2,430k), modular properties for temporary accommodation (£697k), and community/voluntary sector funding (£110k). Total removed: approximately £5.3m. This pattern signals budget pressures elsewhere that required these savings to be withdrawn.
findings.matters: When councils withdraw previously-planned savings, it indicates deteriorating financial position; the true budget problem is being covered by adjustments in Appendix 10, not solved.
findings.figures: £5,322k in identified savings removed or adjusted through Appendix 10
findings.quote: Saving removed though Appendix 10 budget adjustment.

findings.headline: Major adult social care savings depend on service reviews not yet decided
findings.detail: The council is proposing £1,500k savings from a strategic review of its in-house adult social care services (residential care, day services, community meals). The paper explicitly states no decisions have been made yet on the future of these services. Public consultation is still to come. The council is also proposing further reviews of day services (£600k), respite care (£250k), and care package assessments (£2,000k), all status "Budget Recommendation" with delivery uncertain.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether the council can actually deliver its savings plan; a budget that depends on consultations not yet started carries delivery risk.
findings.figures: £1,500k strategic review; £600k day services; £250k respite; £2,000k care package assessments
findings.quote: No decisions have been made yet.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit of £5.8 million will be charged to the General Fund in 2026/27 (£6.9 million Bristol share), adding to budget pressure.
findings.detail: The council must cover a Collection Fund deficit from its 2025/26 balance, meaning it collected less council tax and business rates than budgeted. Of the £5.8 million total deficit, £6.9 million is Bristol's share and will be charged to the General Fund in 2026/27, reducing cash available for services.
findings.matters: A Collection Fund deficit reduces the cash available to fund services at a time when the council is already facing £40.9 million in required savings and a £16.5 million current-year overspend.
findings.figures: Total Collection Fund deficit £5.8m; Bristol's share charged to General Fund in 2026/27 is £6.9m
findings.quote: The Bristol share of this deficit, charged to the General Fund in 2026/27, is £6.9 million.

findings.headline: The HRA rent convergence announcement was delayed and remains unbudgeted; its impact on 2026/27 finances is unknown.
findings.detail: The government was expected to announce rent convergence changes in November 2025 but delayed until January 2026. The paper states: 'the proposed HRA budget for 2026/27 does not include any impacts of rent convergence', and as of the report date, 'an announcement is still to be made'. This creates forecast uncertainty.
findings.matters: An unbudgeted change to rent policy could swing the HRA position by tens of millions. The delay in government announcement means the council cannot quantify the 2026/27 impact, creating forecast risk and the possibility of mid-year budget revision.
findings.figures: HRA revenue budget 2026/27 is £166 million; announcement timing unknown
findings.quote: the proposed HRA budget for 2026/27 does not include any impacts of rent convergence... an announcement is still to be made.

findings.headline: The council must deliver £40.9 million in savings in 2026/27, growing to £70.1 million by 2030/31.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget requires £40.9 million in net service savings to balance, rising to £70.1 million cumulatively over five years. This includes £23.3 million of previously-planned savings plus £17.7 million of new savings. Given that £8.1 million (16%) of current-year savings are already at risk, the growing trajectory creates increasing execution risk.
findings.matters: Large, accelerating savings targets indicate structural budget pressure. When a council is already failing to deliver 16% of current-year savings, a 50% increase in future savings requirements suggests either optimism about delivery or that services will face significant cuts.
findings.figures: £40.9m required in 2026/27; £70.1m by 2030/31; £8.1m of 2025/26's savings at risk
findings.quote: there is a savings requirement of £40.9 million in 2026/27 and £70.1 million by 2030/31.

findings.headline: Business rates now form a larger part of core funding, increasing the council's exposure to local economic movements.
findings.detail: Fair Funding Review 2.0 has consolidated multiple grants into business rates income. The paper states: 'a larger part of the council's overall funding now depends on movements in the local business rates tax base and in-year performance'. Business rates income is £280.4 million in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Shifting from protected grants to volatile business rates increases exposure to the local economy. Any recession reducing business rates collection directly cuts core funding that cannot be immediately offset by service cuts.
findings.figures: Business rates £280.4 million in 2026/27, rising to £333.1 million by 2030/31
findings.quote: This means that a larger part of the council's overall funding now depends on movements in the local business rates tax base and in-year performance.

findings.headline: Council is forecasting a £16.5 million overspend (2.9%) in 2025/26, with £8.1 million of savings at risk.
findings.detail: At Period 8, the council forecast a £16.5 million overspend (2.9% of budget) driven by Children's (£11.4m) and Adult Social Care (£5.3m). Of £51.3 million savings target, only 84% is forecast to deliver, with £8.1 million (16%) at risk. This shows current-year budget stress in demand-led services.
findings.matters: A 2.9% current-year overspend plus undelivered savings increase the risk that problems roll forward into 2026/27, making next year's £40.9 million savings target harder to achieve.
findings.figures: £16.5 million overspend; Children £11.4m, Adult Social Care £5.3m; £8.1m of £51.3m savings at risk
findings.quote: At Period 8 2025/26, the council forecast an end of year overspend of £16.5 million (2.9%)... with £8.1 million (16%) at risk of non-delivery in year.

findings.headline: HRA received a Regulatory Judgment in July 2024 finding serious failings in landlord standards.
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a July 2024 judgment finding 'serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the Safety and Quality Standard and significant improvement is needed'. This is a material governance and compliance finding in the council's largest ringfenced account.
findings.matters: Regulatory findings of serious failings signal governance risk. If regulator escalates intervention, it could trigger special measures affecting the £166m revenue and £180m capital HRA account.
findings.figures: £166 million HRA revenue budget 2026/27; £180.2 million HRA capital budget
findings.quote: In July 2024, the Regulator issued a Regulatory Judgment and concluded that there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the Safety and Quality Standard and significant improvement is needed.

findings.headline: DSG deficit is now £68.5 million and the council is off-track to meet its legal 2030 deadline to eliminate it.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is forecast at £68.5 million by end 2025/26. The council has a Safety Valve Agreement with the DfE requiring elimination by 31 March 2030, but is 'not currently on track' to meet this deadline. The paper does not explain the path to recovery.
findings.matters: A £68.5 million structural deficit in education that is off-track to resolve by government deadline signals both governance weakness and a potential contingent liability.
findings.figures: £68.5 million by end 2025/26; £73.6 million by end 2026/27; target elimination by 31 March 2030
findings.quote: The council is not currently on track to eliminate the DSG deficit by 31 March 2030, as required in the Safety Valve Agreement with the DfE.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Council drew £8.6m from revenue reserves in 2025/26 to fund transformation; replenishment depends on future capital receipts materialising
findings.detail: Table 1 shows £8.6m was funded from 'Temporary Use of Revenue Reserves' in 2025/26 (54% of that year's transformation financing). The strategy states this is temporary: 'The anticipated use of revenue reserves in 2025/26 is planned to be replenished from applying additional capital receipts in future to support transformational schemes.' This creates a double dependency: future disposal receipts must both fund the transformation pipeline AND rebuild reserves.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown signals financial stress and reduces the council's financial flexibility. If capital receipts disappoint, reserves stay depleted and the council has less buffer for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: £8.6m from reserves in 2025/26, total 2025/26 transformation spend £15.8m
findings.quote: The anticipated use of revenue reserves in 2025/26 is planned to be replenished from applying additional capital receipts in future to support transformational schemes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Council must generate £71.5m from asset disposals over five years; disposals are fully committed by end 2025/26 and failure to deliver disposals will force programme cuts
findings.detail: The council estimates it will have 'fully applied its capital receipts' by end of 2025/26 (line 1.21). It then requires £71.5m in capital receipts over the MTFS period to fund capital programmes and transformation. The strategy explicitly warns: 'Should the disposal programme not progress as currently profiled other funding sources will need to be identified or programmes and projects reduced' (line 1.23). The remaining unmet need after 2026/27 is £70.2m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's capital programmes depend entirely on delivering a disposal pipeline. Any shortfall in asset sales forces either higher borrowing or programme cuts; there is no budget contingency.
findings.figures: £71.5m required over five years, £70.2m remaining after 2026/27, capital receipts fully applied by 31 March 2026
findings.quote: Should the disposal programme not progress as currently profiled other funding sources will need to be identified or programmes and projects reduced.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5 - Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Strategy
findings.headline: Capital receipts flexibility directive ends 2029/30 with no guaranteed extension; council working to reduce dependency but plans £20m transformation spend in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council's strategy relies on a government directive allowing capital receipts to fund transformation costs, running through 2029/30. Council explicitly acknowledges the directive may not extend further and states it is 'working towards reducing reliance on Flexible Use of Capital Receipts'. Yet the 2026/27 plan requires £20.0m for transformation via this mechanism, with £42.5m total capital receipts needed that year.
findings.matters: If the directive is not extended, the council loses a key funding mechanism and may face acute budget pressures in the final year of its medium-term financial strategy (2029/30) unless alternative funds are identified beforehand.
findings.figures: £20.0m transformation (2026/27), £42.5m total capital receipts requirement (2026/27), flexibility runs through 2029/30
findings.quote: should no further extensions be made to the directive, in the final year of the Medium Term Financial Strategy the council is able to manage continued transformation and improvement without this application

findings.paper_title: 9 Appendix 1 Grant Thornton ISA 260 Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: DSG deficit of £6.7m in current year plus £2.6m prior year surplus being funded from council reserves rather than schools budget
findings.detail: The audit identified an adjustment of £9.275m where the Council is holding Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit contributions (£6.699m current year and £2.576m prior year surplus) in an earmarked reserve rather than applying them to DSG expenditure in 2025/26. This shows the Council is building a reserve to absorb schools overspending, delaying the impact on the schools budget.
findings.matters: DSG deficits indicate the schools system is overspending its budget. By holding the deficit in an earmarked reserve, the Council is deferring the budget reality until future years when it must either cut schools or find other revenue. This signals budget pressure in an essential service.
findings.figures: £6.699m DSG deficit 2024/25; £2.576m prior year DSG surplus adjustment; £9.275m total reserve adjustment
findings.quote: One adjustment was identified which reduced usable earmarked reserves and increased unusable reserves of £9.275m. This is due to Council contributions to the dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit (£6.699m) and the prior year DSG surplus (£2.576m) being held in an earmarked reserve rather than being applied to the DSG expenditure in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 9 Appendix 1 Grant Thornton ISA 260 Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Pension liability position swings to £62.8m net liability after first-time application of IFRS 14 asset ceiling
findings.detail: The Council's Local Government Pension Scheme position changed materially in 2024/25 due to application of an IFRS 14 asset ceiling for the first time. Before the ceiling was applied, the Council had a £0.8m surplus position. After the ceiling, the reported position is a £62.8m net liability. This technical accounting treatment significantly affects the reported net liabilities on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a significant claim on the council's financial position. A £63.6m swing in position materially changes balance sheet strength and affects net worth available for repayment of other obligations. Lenders need to understand this liability is now locked in.
findings.figures: £0.8m surplus before IFRIC 14; £62.8m net liability after
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Councils pension net defined liability position was impacted by an IFRIC 14 asset ceiling. Prior to the asset ceiling being applied, the Council had a LGPS surplus position of £0.8m. After the application of the asset celling, the Councils reported position for the LGPS is a net liability of £62.8m.

findings.paper_title: 9 Appendix 1 Grant Thornton ISA 260 Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Loss of experienced finance staff has caused audit delays and forced restatement of accounts; additional fees will be charged
findings.detail: Audit completion was delayed from September 2025 to December 2025 because loss of key experienced finance officers prevented timely provision of good quality working papers and responses to audit queries. This required significant additional audit procedures and additional fees. Progress improved after mid-September when the Council allocated more resources and hired a new Finance Business Partner.
findings.matters: Loss of financial expertise directly reduces the council's capacity to manage money, produce timely accounts, and respond to audit challenges. Additional costs impact the council's financial position. Future audit processes depend on rebuilding this capacity.
findings.figures: Audit delayed 3 months (September to December 2025); additional unquantified fees
findings.quote: due to the loss of some experienced members of the finance team and the impact that this has had on providing high quality supporting evidence in a timely way, and due to the IFRS16 issue highlighted above, the completion of the audit has been delayed. As at the date of this report, we have yet to commence our detailed review of IFRS 16

findings.paper_title: 9 Appendix 1 Grant Thornton ISA 260 Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Auditor identified significant weakness in Council's financial sustainability arrangements
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's value-for-money work identified a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements for securing financial sustainability and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. The auditor is formally not satisfied the Council has proper arrangements in place. This was reported separately in October 2025 in the Auditor's Annual Report.
findings.matters: A VFM significant weakness in financial sustainability is a formal audit concern about whether the council can sustain operations. This directly affects credit risk assessment and signals management capability issues.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: We identified a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements and so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources in respect of financial sustainability and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: 9 Appendix 1 Grant Thornton ISA 260 Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease obligations materially understated in published draft accounts; now estimated at c.£52m
findings.detail: Bristol published unaudited draft accounts on 27 June 2025 without recording IFRS 16 lease adjustments, claiming impact would be immaterial (£2.4m). After audit challenge, the Council discovered the actual impact is material: right-of-use assets now estimated at approximately £52m. Final working papers are still pending and detailed testing has not yet commenced.
findings.matters: A £52m understatement of lease obligations is material to the balance sheet and directly affects the Council's reported financial position. Lenders assessing repayment capacity and asset coverage need accurate, complete liability information.
findings.figures: Initially estimated £2.4m; revised estimate c.£52m right-of-use asset total
findings.quote: The Council published their draft accounts on the 27 June 2025 without reflecting the impact on IFRS 16 within these. At the time of publishing, the Council had estimated that the impact of IFRS 16 would not be material (right of use asset closing balance £2.4m)... The Council's current calculation estimate a material impact on the financial statements with an estimated right of use asset total of c.£52m
